title: UNSEEN PHILIPPINES | The Unseen Mountain Worlds Lost in Time
fullText: In the mountains of the Philippines, there is a woman who is over 106 years old. She sits on a wooden bench outside a HUD with no electricity, dips a thorn attached to a bamboo stick into a pot of charcoal and citrus ink, and taps a pattern into human skin that has not changed in a thousand years. People fly from Tokyo, from Berlin, from Los Angeles, and hike for hours through mountain trails with no cell phone signal to sit in front of her. She is the last person alive who knows the original patterns. When she dies, a tradition older than most countries on Earth dies with her. In another place, farmers have been growing rice on the sides of mountains for 2,000 years. Without [music] a single pump, without a single machine, the water flows from the top of the mountain to the bottom through a network of channels carved [music] by hand into rock and clay, terrace by terrace, generation after generation. The system still works, but the young people are leaving for Manila. And the terraces, 2,000 years of them, are beginning to collapse. On one island, there are more volcanoes [music] per square kilometer than anywhere else on Earth. One of them erupted and sank a cemetery beneath the sea. The crosses are still visible underwater. Fishermen row over them every morning. And in the Cordiera Mountains, there is a village where the dead are not buried. They are placed in wooden coffins, and the coffins are nailed to the face of a cliff hundreds of meters above the valley. Some have been hanging there for over 2,000 years. The oldest ones have rotted open. You can see the bones inside. These are not tourist destinations. Most Filipinos have never been to any of them. This is the Philippines that nobody shows you. The mountain worlds that exist [music] above the beaches, above the resorts, above the postcard version of the country, and almost every one of them is disappearing. Before we start, drop a comment telling us where you are watching from right now. We want to see how many countries this video reaches. Mount Pulag, Benet Province, Cordiierra. At 2,926 m above sea level, Mount Pulag is the third highest peak in the Philippines. It sits in the Cordiera central mountain range of northern Luzon, a region so removed from the coastal lands that the Spanish colonial government never fully [music] controlled it. The Abaloy and Kankanai peoples who live on its slopes governed themselves for centuries. The summit of Pulag is grassland, not jungle, not rock, grass. Rolling fields of dwarf bamboo grass that turn gold in the dry season, stretching across the ridge line like a landscape from the Scottish Highlands dropped into the tropics. According to the Department of Environment and Natural Resources, Mount Pulag is classified as a national park and is home to the largest remaining mossy forest in Luzon, a cloud forest where every branch is wrapped in moss so thick that the trees look upholstered. But the thing that draws people to Pulag is what happens at dawn. The mountain sits above the cloud line. On clear mornings, climbers who camp at the summit grassland wake up surrounded by a sea of clouds that stretches [music] to every horizon. The clouds fill the valleys below completely, smooth, white, unbroken, and the mountain peaks of the cordiiera rise through them like islands in a white ocean. The temperature at the summit drops below zero at night. [music] According to Pagasa, the Philippine National Weather Service, Pulag is one of the only places in the Philippines where frost [music] forms naturally. In a tropical country where the lowland average is 32° C, the summit of Pulog gets cold enough to freeze the water in your bottle. The Abbaloy people who live on the lower slopes consider the mountains sacred. According to ethnographic research published by the University [music] of the Philippines Bagio, the Abaloy believe Mount Pulag is the resting place of their ancestors spirits. Certain areas of the mountain are traditionally off limits. The grassland summit where the tourists now camp was historically visited only by ritual leaders. A [music] tropical country with a frozen mountaintop. A sea of clouds at dawn that makes the entire world below disappear. And a people who considered the summit sacred long before anyone [music] brought a camera. Sagata hanging coffins. Mountain province Cordiiera. In the limestone cliffs above the town of Sagada in the mountain province of northern Luzon, wooden coffins are nailed to the rock face. Some are wedged into natural crevices. Others are suspended from wooden pegs driven into the cliff. They hang at heights ranging from 10 to over a 100 meters above the valley floor. Some of the coffins are recent smooth wood, clearly constructed within the last few decades. Others have been there so long [music] that the wood has rotted through. The lids have fallen away. The bones inside are visible from below. According to anthropological research published by the National Museum of the Philippines, the practice of cliff burial among the Eagorote people of the Cordillera dates back at least 2,000 years. The tradition is rooted in the belief that placing the dead at elevation brings them closer to the ancestral spirits and protects the body from floods, animals, and enemies. The process is specific. According to accounts collected by the Mountain Province Cultural Heritage Office, elderly eagerote who sense death approaching will sometimes carve their own coffins in advance. The body is placed in a seated fetal position, the same position it occupied in the womb. The coffin is then carried up the cliff by family members and secured to the rock. The route up is often unmarked, a scramble over limestone with the coffin on the carrier's backs. The practice has not stopped. It has slowed. Younger generations increasingly choose lowland style burial. But according to community leaders interviewed by the Philippine Daily Inquirer in 2019, cliff burials still occur in Sagada. The most recent documented hanging coffin was placed within the last decade. Visitors who stand at the base of Echo Valley in Sagada and look up see dozens of coffins at various stages of decay. Some intact, some [music] skeletal, some just fragments of wood clinging to the rock. The oldest ones are barely distinguishable [music] from the cliff itself. The newest ones still smell of fresh cut pine. 2,000 years of placing the dead above the living. A tradition that predates Christianity in the Philippines by over a millennium. And a cliff face that holds the remains of people who were [music] born before the Spanish ever arrived. Still hanging above a valley where their descendants grow rice and send their children to a school with internet. Mount Pinatubo, Zambales and Tarlac provinces, central Luzon. On June 15th, [music] 1991, Mount Pinatubo erupted with a force that the US Geological Survey classified as the second largest volcanic [music] eruption of the 20th century. The eruption column reached 35 km into the atmosphere. According to USGS volcanologist Chris Newu-Whall, who was part of the monitoring team, the eruption ejected roughly 10 [music] cubic kilm of material, enough to bury the entire island of Manhattan under a layer of ash 40 m [music] deep. The eruption killed over 800 people directly. According to data compiled by the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology [music] known as Fiulks, the subsequent laahar rivers of volcanic mud formed when rain mixed with the loose ash deposits killed hundreds more over the following years. Entire towns were buried. The Ietta people, the indigenous inhabitants of the mountain slopes, lost their ancestral lands completely. According to the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples, roughly 30,000 [music] Ieta were displaced. Many have never returned. The eruption also had a global effect that most people outside of atmospheric science have never heard of. According to NASA's Gddard Institute for Space Studies, the sulfur dioxide injected into the stratosphere by Pinatubo formed a layer of aerosol particles that reflected [music] sunlight away from the Earth's surface. Global temperatures dropped by roughly 0.5° C for the following 2 years. The eruption of a single mountain in the Philippines measurably cooled the entire planet. Today, the crater holds a lake, turquoise, [music] roughly 2 and 1/2 km across. The color comes from dissolved minerals in the water, sulfur, iron, and volcanic sediment. According to 5 vols monitoring data, the lake has no outlet. It fills with rain and volcanic seepage and sits in the crater like a bowl of blue green paint. Reaching the lake requires a trek through laahar fields, flat gray plains of hardened volcanic mud where rivers have carved canyons 20 m deep. The landscape looks like the surface of the moon. No vegetation, no color, just gray in every direction until the crater rim appears and the turquoise water [music] below it shocks you into remembering that color exists. A volcano that cooled the planet. A lake the color of nothing else on Earth. and an indigenous people who lost their mountain and have spent three decades trying to get it back. Lake Holone, [music] South Kotabato, Mindanao. On the summit of Mount Parker, a dormant volcano in southern Mindanao, there is a lake that has no road to it, no trail markers, no signs. To reach it, you [music] hike for roughly 5 hours through dense tropical forest, ascending from the lowland heat into the cooler air of the volcanic highlands. The Tiboli people control [music] access. According to the South Kotabato Provincial Tourism Office, any visitor who wishes to reach [music] Lake Hog must register with the Tiboli community, pay a conservation fee, and be accompanied by a local guide. There is no way around this. The trails are unmarked, and the Tiboli know paths through [music] the forest that are not visible to outsiders. Lake Halog sits at roughly 1,800 m above sea level in the caldera of Mount Parker. The water is cold, clear, and surrounded on all sides by forest [music] that drops steeply down to the lake shore. There are no buildings, no docks, no boats. According to limnological surveys conducted by Mindanao State University, the lake is roughly 1.5 km across and reaches [music] depths of over 60 m. The water quality is among the highest of any freshwater body in the Philippines. A consequence of the lake having no agricultural runoff, no settlements, and no road access. The Tiboli relationship with the lake is not recreational. According to ethnographic research by Dr. Sarah Deal Hunt of Atineo de Dvao University, the Tiboli consider [music] the lake and the surrounding forest to be spiritually significant. The forest [music] is not a park. It is a living boundary. The Tiboli have resisted multiple attempts by commercial interests to develop the area, including a proposal in the early 2000s to [music] build a road to the lake for tourism. The proposal was rejected. The Tiboli argument documented in [music] provincial government minutes was simple. A road would bring volume. Volume would bring waste. Waste would kill the lake. They chose the 5-hour [music] hike. They chose controlled access. They chose to keep the lake exactly as it has been for as long as anyone can remember. A crater lake on a dormant [music] volcano guarded not by fences or rangers, but by a people who decided that the hardest way to reach something is sometimes the only way to keep it alive. Mount Hamigitan, Dvau oriental, Mindanao. On the eastern coast of Mindanao, rising from the Pacific facing [music] lowlands, a mountain ridge reaches 1,637 m. The lower slopes are tropical rainforest. [music] The mid elevations are mossy cloud forest and the summit. The summit is something else entirely. [music] At the top of Mount Hamigitan, the trees are no more than a meter tall, bonsai sized, twisted, gnarled. Their roots grip exposed rock and thin acidic soil. Their trunks are wrapped in moss. According to the UNESCO World Heritage Committee, which inscribed the Mount Hamigitan Range Wildlife Sanctuary in 2014, the Summit Pygmy Forest is one of the most biologically distinct ecosystems in Southeast Asia. The stunting is caused by the extreme conditions at the summit. High winds, poor soil, high acidity, and UV exposure. According to botanical surveys published by the Philippine National Museum, the trees are not young. Some are estimated to be over a hundred years old. They have simply grown as much as the environment will allow, which is barely anything at all. The mountain hold species found nowhere else on Earth. According to the International Union for Conservation of Nature, the Philippine pygmy woodpecker, the Hamigitan hairyle pitcher [music] plant, one of the largest pitcher plants in the world, capable of trapping rodents, and several species of frog discovered only on this single mountain, have been documented by researchers from the Philippine Eagle Foundation and the Harry Foundation. The mountain sits in a typhoon corridor. According to data from Pagasa, Dvau Oriental is one of the most typhoon struck [music] provinces in the Philippines. In December 2012, typhoon Bopa struck the region with sustained winds of 175 km per hour. [music] Over a thousand people died in that surrounding lowlands. The pygmy forest on the summit survived. The trees are too short and too flexible for the wind to break. They have been bending in typhoons for centuries. A forest of 100-year-old trees that are smaller than a child. Plants that eat rats. Species that exist on one mountain and nowhere [music] else. And a summit that has survived every typhoon the Pacific has thrown at it by refusing to grow tall enough to be noticed. Buscalan village, Kolinga province, Cordillera. In the Kolinga province of the northern Cordillera, on a mountain ridge that requires a 1-hour hike from the nearest road, there is a village of roughly 300 people where a woman has been tattooing human skin for over 90 years. Her name is Wang Odd Oay. She was born around 1917. The exact date is uncertain because birth records in the Kinga Highlands were not kept during the American colonial period. As of [music] 2026, she is believed to be over 106 years old. According to the National Commission for Culture in the Arts, which recognized her as a national [music] living treasure in 2018, Wang Odd is the oldest Mamba Bat, a traditional Kinga handtap tattoo artist [music] and the last surviving practitioner who learned the art directly from the original lineage. The technique has not changed in a thousand years. A thorn from a calamani or pomelo tree is attached to a thin bamboo stick. The ink is a mixture [music] of charcoal and water. Wang odd taps the thorn into the skin with a second stick dot by dot without stencil without guidelines. Working from memory and from patterns that were taught to her by her father when she was a teenager. According to anthropological documentation [music] by Dr. Analin Salvador Amorez of the University of the Philippines Bagio. The original Kingolinga tattoo tradition was not decorative. The patterns were earned. Warriors received specific designs after taking a head in battle. Women received fertility patterns. Each tattoo was a record, a biography written on the body. Wang Odd was not supposed to be the last. She trained apprentices throughout her life, but the Kinga Highlands depopulated over the decades as young people left for lowland cities. According to Kinga provincial government records, the population of remote mountain baron guys has declined by over 40% since the 1980s. [music] Two of Wang Odd's grand nieces, Grace and Elang, are now learning the craft. [music] They practice daily. But according to interviews published by CNN Philippines, they have acknowledged that some of the oldest patterns, the ones Wang Odd carries in her memory, but is [music] not yet transferred, may not survive the transition. Tourists arrive in Buscolan daily. They hike for an hour up a trail with no guard rails, [music] wait in line on a wooden bench, and receive a tattoo from a woman born before commercial aviation existed. She charges roughly 1,000 pesos, about $18. The tattoo takes between 10 and [music] 40 minutes. The sound is a rhythmic tapping, thorn on bamboo on skin that echoes [music] off the stone walls of the hut and carries down the valley. A thousand years of tradition. One woman who remembers it all and two young women learning as fast as they can in a race against a clock that no one wants to acknowledge is running. Kamigin [music] Island, northern Mindanao. In the Boho Sea, roughly 10 km off the northern coast of Mindanao, there is an island that measures roughly 238 [music] km. It has seven volcanoes, more volcanoes per square kilmter than any other island in the world. The most recent eruption was [music] Mount Hebach in 1953. According to PHIVOLCS historical records, pyrolastic flows raced down the mountains slopes and killed roughly [music] 500 people in the surrounding villages. The town of Mambajao, the [music] island's capital, was partially destroyed. But the eruption that left the most visible scar happened earlier. In the 1870s, a volcanic event triggered the sinking [music] of a portion of the island's coastal land near the old town of Catan. A cemetery slid beneath the sea. The old Cataman [music] Cemetery is now a coralcovered underwater site roughly 200 m offshore. According to the Kamagin Provincial Tourism Office, the stone crosses and grave markers are still visible. Standing upright on the seafloor in roughly 3 to 5 m of water. Coral has grown on them. Fish swim between them. The names on some of the markers are [music] still legible. Fishermen row over the sunken cemetery every morning. The graves of their own ancestors are beneath their boats. According to community interviews documented by the University of the Philippines Visayas, the fishermen regard the site with a specific kind of familiarity that outsiders find unsettling. They point casually to spots in the water. My greatgrandfather [music] is there. The way someone in another country might point to a plot in a churchyard. The island has rebuilt after every eruption. The 1953 disaster destroyed much of Mamba [music] Jao. According to the Philippine Statistics Authority, the population today is roughly 90,000. They live on an island with seven volcanoes, at least [music] three of which Fivolks classifies as potentially active. The volcanic soil grows coconut, cacao, and rice with yields that surpass most of the surrounding region. Seven volcanoes, one island, a cemetery underwater, and 90,000 people whose daily calculation is the same one humans have been making on volcanic islands for millennia. The soil is too good to leave, and the mountain has been quiet long enough to trust. Mount Oppo, Dva region, Mindanao. At 2,954 [music] m, Mount Oppo is the highest point in the Philippines. The Bobo Tagaba [music] people, the indigenous inhabitants of its slopes, call it Apo Sandawa, the grandfather of all mountains. According to oral traditions documented by the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples, [music] the mountain is the dwelling place of Mandarangan, the god of war and justice. Climbing to the summit without proper respect is considered a provocation. The mountain is also the last significant habitat [music] of the Philippine eagle. With a wingspan exceeding 2 m, the Philippine eagle is the largest eagle in the world by wing surface area. According to the Philippine Eagle Foundation, which has monitored the population since the 1970s, fewer than 800 individuals remain in the wild. The species is classified as critically endangered by the IUCN. Killing a Philippine eagle carries a penalty of up [music] to 12 years in prison under Philippine law, the harshest protection for any single species [music] in the country. The eagle's nest in the old growth diproarp forest on Mount Oppo's mid-elevation slopes. A single breeding pair requires a territory of roughly 25 to 50 square kilmters of continuous forest. According to research published by the Philippine Eagle Foundation in the journal Biological Conservation, [music] the deforestation rate in Mindanao has reduced available habitat by over 70% [music] since the 1970s. Each nesting pair that loses its territory does not relocate. It disappears. The Bobo Tagaba have been the eagle's most effective protectors. According to the foundation's field teams, the indigenous community monitors nesting sites and [music] reports illegal logging activity. The relationship is not sentimental. According to BooBo oral tradition, the eagle is a messenger of Mandarangan. Harming one invites consequences that no legal penalty can match. The highest mountain in a country of 7,000 islands, an eagle too large to believe, and an indigenous people whose spiritual framework has done more for conservation than any government program. Because when you believe the bird is a messenger from a god, you do not need a law to stop you from killing it. Mount Mayon, Albe province, [music] Belell region. Mount Mayon is a strat volcano on the island of Luzon, roughly 330 km southeast of Manila. Its elevation is 2,462 [music] m. Its base to summit symmetry has been described by the Smithsonian Institution's Global Volcanism Program as the most perfectly conical large volcanic [music] structure on Earth. The cone is so symmetrical that it has become the visual icon of the Philippines. It appears on currency, on government [music] seals, on tourism materials. Seen from the surrounding lowlands on a clear day, the profile is almost geometrically perfect. a single unbroken line from base to summit against the sky. It is also one of the most active and destructive volcanoes in the Philippines. According to Fivolks, Mayon has erupted over 50 times since 1616, making it the most frequently erupting volcano in the Philippine archipelago. The most devastating eruption occurred on February 1st, 1814 when pyrolastic flows and laahars destroyed the town of Kagzawa. According to church records preserved by the Dascese of Lagospi, roughly 1,200 people died, many of them inside the Kagawa [music] church where they had taken shelter believing the stone walls would protect them. The walls [music] did not protect them. The pyrolastic flow was traveling at over 100 kmh and at temperatures exceeding 700° C, the church was buried. Today, only the bell tower is visible above the solidified laahar. It [music] rises from a flat field of gray volcanic rock, a single stone finger pointing [music] at the mountain that buried everything around it. According to Fivolks, the most recent significant eruption [music] was in January 2018 when the volcano produced ash plumes reaching 10 km and lava flows that descended 2 km from the summit. Over 90,000 people were evacuated from the surrounding danger zones. According to the Albay Provincial Disaster [music] Risk Reduction and Management Office, some families have been evacuated and returned more than a dozen times in their lifetimes. The evacuations follow a pattern. Alert level rises, families pack, evacuation [music] centers fill, the volcano quiets, families return, they replant, the children go back to school, the volcano rumbles again. According to interviews conducted by Rapler in 2018, one farmer from Barangai [music] Mabinit less than 8 kilometers from the crater said he had been evacuated 11 times. He returned each time. The soil he said is the best in Albe. [music] The Kagawa bell tower is now a tourist attraction. Visitors pose for photographs with the tower in the foreground and the perfect cone of Mayan in the background. The tower where,200 people died in 1814 is now a selfie spot with the same volcano that killed them rising behind it. Perfectly shaped, perfectly patient. Bonawi rice terraces. Ephuga province, [music] Cordiiera. In the Cordiiera Mountains of Northern Luzon, carved into the steep slopes of the Ephuga Highlands, the Bonawi [music] rice terraces have been called the eighth wonder of the world. Not by engineers, not by architects, by the people who first saw them. and could not understand how they were possible. The terraces cover approximately 10,000 hectares of mountainside. They rise from valley floors to ridge lines at elevations exceeding 1,500 m. If laid end to end, according to estimates by the Philippine Department of Tourism, the terrace walls would stretch roughly halfway around the earth. [music] They were built by hand. No machinery, no draft animals on the steepest sections. Stone and clay walls, some reaching over [music] 15 meters in height, constructed by the Ephuga people beginning roughly 2,000 years ago. According to archaeological research [music] published by the University of the Philippines Archaeological Studies Program, the construction was not a single project. It was a continuous process spanning centuries with each generation adding, maintaining, and extending the work of the previous one. The irrigation system is what makes the terraces extraordinary beyond their visual impact. Water flows from the mountaintop forests through a network of channels, bamboo pipes, and handcarved stone aqueducts, descending terrace by terrace in a gravity-fed system that [music] requires no pumps, no valves, and no external power source. According to hydraulic analysis published by the International Rice Research Institute, the system distributes water across thousands of individual patties at different elevations with remarkable precision. The forests at the top of the watershed are considered sacred. Cutting them is prohibited by traditional ephuga law. Not for environmental reasons as the modern world understands them, but because the Ephuga understood 2,000 years ago that without the forest, the water [music] stops, and without the water, the terraces die. The terraces are dying anyway. According to a 2012 report by the Ephuga Cultural Heritage Office, roughly [music] 30% of the rice terraces have been damaged or abandoned. The cause is not geological, it is demographic. Young Ephuga are leaving the highlands for [music] Manila for Baguio for overseas work. According to the Philippine Statistics Authority, the population of Ephuga province has stagnated while surrounding land provinces have grown. The maintenance of the terraces requires constant laborintensive work. Rebuilding walls after every monsoon, clearing channels, replanting by hand in need water on slopes where a misstep can send you sliding 10 [music] m down a stone face. According to UNESCO, which inscribed the rice terraces of the Philippine cordiieras as a world heritage site in 1995 and placed them on the list of world heritage endanger in 2001, the terraces represent one of the most significant examples of sustainable agriculture in human history. The 2001 danger listing cited the abandonment of terraces by younger generations as the primary threat. The terraces were removed from the danger list [music] in 2012 after the Philippine government implemented conservation programs. But according to follow-up assessments by the International Council [music] on Monuments and Sites, the underlying trend has not reversed. The young people [music] are still leaving. The terraces still require the same amount of labor. And the people who know how to do the work, [music] how to read the water, how to set a stone wall that holds for a century, how to time the planting with the rain and the elevation are in their 60s and 70s. There is a specific moment in the Ephoga agricultural calendar [music] called the Ubu, a communal work period when families from neighboring terraces join together to repair walls, clear channels, and prepare the patties for planting. According to Ephuga elder testimonies collected by the save the Ephuga [music] terraces movement, the ubu was once a festival. Hundreds of people working the terraces together, singing the sound of stone on stone carrying across the valley. The ubu still happens, but the songs are quieter now. The [music] hands are fewer, and the terraces that took 2,000 years to build are losing a race with a generation that discovered there are easier ways to make a living than standing kneedeep in a patty on the side of a mountain, repairing a wall that their great great great grandparents built and their children may never see. 2,000 years of carving mountains into staircases of water and rice. No blueprints, no engineers, no government funding, just hands and stone and a belief that what you build should last longer [music] than you do. The terraces are still there. The water still flows. The system still works. [music] The same system, the same channels, the same physics, but the people who understand [music] it are getting older. And the mountains are patient. They were there before the terraces. They will be there after. The Philippines has 7,641 [music] islands. Most of the world knows the beaches, the resorts, the white sand that appears on magazine [music] covers. But above the coastline, in the mountains, in the volcanic highlands, in the cloud forests and the [music] river valleys that the tourism boards do not print on brochures, there is a country that most people have never seen. A frozen mountaintop in the tropics, where the clouds become a sea at dawn. coffins nailed to a cliff face 2,000 years ago with fresh [music] ones still being added. A volcano that cooled the entire planet and left a turquoise [music] lake in its crater. A lake on a dormant volcano guarded by a people who chose [music] a 5-hour hike over a road. A forest of hundred-year-old trees that are shorter than a child. A woman tapping ink into skin with a thorn and a stick carrying a thousand years of patterns in her memory. An island with seven volcanoes and a cemetery underwater. An eagle too large to believe protected by a people who think it carries messages from a god. A perfect cone that is buried towns [music] and become a selfie backdrop. And a staircase of rice patties carved into mountains by hand, 2,000 years old, still [music] working, slowly being abandoned by the generation that inherited it. The beaches are not going anywhere. These places might be. Which one would you want to see before it changes forever? Tell us in the comments. And if you made it to the end, you already know this channel is for you. Hit subscribe, turn on notifications. The next video takes you somewhere even more impossible. We will see you there.
fullTextVi: Ở vùng núi Philippines có người phụ nữ hơn 106 tuổi tuổi. Cô ngồi trên chiếc ghế gỗ bên ngoài HUD không có điện, nhúng gai cắm vào que tre cho vào nồi than và mực cam, và chạm vào da người một hình mẫu không thay đổi trong hàng nghìn năm năm. Mọi người bay từ Tokyo, từ Berlin, từ Los Angeles và đi bộ hàng giờ qua những con đường mòn trên núi không có tín hiệu điện thoại di động để ngồi trước mặt cô. Cô ấy là người cuối cùng còn sống biết được nguyên mẫu ban đầu. Khi cô qua đời, một truyền thống lâu đời hơn hầu hết các quốc gia trên Trái đất cũng chết theo cô. Ở một nơi khác, nông dân trồng lúa trên sườn núi 2.000 năm. Không có [âm nhạc] một chiếc máy bơm, không một chiếc máy, nước sẽ chảy từ đỉnh núi xuống chân núi qua mạng lưới kênh rạch [âm nhạc] bằng tay thành đá và đất sét, hết tầng này đến tầng khác, thế hệ này qua thế hệ khác. Hệ thống vẫn hoạt động nhưng những người trẻ tuổi đang rời đi Manila. Và những bậc thang, trong số đó đã 2.000 năm tuổi, đang bắt đầu sụp đổ. Trên một hòn đảo, có nhiều núi lửa [âm nhạc] trên mỗi km vuông hơn bất kỳ nơi nào khác trên Trái đất. Một trong số chúng phun trào và đánh chìm một nghĩa trang dưới biển. Những cây thánh giá vẫn còn nhìn thấy được dưới nước. Ngư dân chèo thuyền qua chúng mỗi sáng. Và ở dãy núi Cordiera, có một ngôi làng không có người chết bị chôn vùi.
